chapters.fx: What to watch: the Sunday 5pm ET FX reopen — the first market test of the evening's news (wider risk-off gap or hold). Then the weekend dead zone; the next real test is CPI Wednesday Oct 14, 7:30am CT — core m/m of 0.2% or below validates disinflation; 0.3%+ revives October (currently ~18%).
chapters.meaning: What changed: the 4pm edition couldn't see Friday evening — and the evening delivered two curveballs. Iran struck the Trafigura-chartered VLCC Gem No 2 off the UAE and the IRGC officially claimed the NV Sunshine hit, warning of 'punishment' across the region — the strike campaign is widening beyond Hormuz. Brent settled at $104.72 (+2.4% on the week). Then came the Trump–Putin diesel deal: Russia supplies 300k tons of diesel immediately, up to ~4.8M tons in sequence, with a Treasury general license lifting Russian oil sanctions for diesel through April 7, 2027 — the first Russian energy imports into the US since 2022. Diesel fell 3%. Thread: the hawkish hold is in week four — FOMC minutes had 'most' officials seeing another hike by year-end, Dec is ~82% priced and October ~18% (CME, via Reuters), claims held 197k for a fourth straight week. Fed's Collins spoke ~3pm CT but no wire coverage exists — treat her remarks as unpriced. What it means: confirms the thesis, with a twist. The diesel deal is a mild disinflationary tailwind through the fuel-inflation channel the Fed watches — but the volumes (~6M barrels, ≈1.5 days of US demand, per Pickering via CNN) make it more politics than game-changer. Meanwhile the evening's escalation puts a floor under oil — and under the energy-driven inflation floor beneath December pricing. The dollar barely moved (DXY ~102.0–102.2, −0.3% Friday), which is the market saying Friday's data changed nothing and the evening changed only the edges.

chapters.fx: What to watch: the French budget plenary Tuesday Oct 13 (key votes run late Nov–mid Dec), German ZEW the same day, and the Aa3 rating review this month. On the chart, 1.1161 is the line: a break risks 1.1065; a hold plus fading fiscal fear opens a relief bounce toward 1.13.
chapters.meaning: What changed: nothing market-moving overnight — the euro chapter is the quiet one this edition, and it's worth saying so plainly. EUR/USD closed ~1.12 (−0.1% Friday), holding above Monday's 17-month low of 1.1161, on course for a fifth straight weekly fall. The fiscal dossier thickened: debt/GDP 119.3% in 2026 rising to 121.7% in 2027, the 2026 growth forecast cut to 0.5%, EU finance ministers in Luxembourg pressing Paris to move faster, the ECB's TPI effectively off the table for an excessive-deficit country, and the IMF's Georgieva telling France to cut the deficit to regain confidence. Thread: four weeks of French fiscal stress layered onto ECB-policy drag; the 4pm edition said the relief-bounce hope broke, and Friday's tape says the bleeding paused, not reversed — the OAT–Bund spread sits ~140–146bp, off the 150bp+ wides. What it means: confirms the prior thesis — the fiscal risk premium is still priced in, and the dollar-side of this pair (see the USD chapter) is doing the rest. A quiet euro is the market waiting for Tuesday.

chapters.meaning: What changed: very little — GBP/USD closed ~1.324, essentially flat Friday, and sterling kept its 16-month high against the euro at 84.74p, a second straight weekly gain vs the single currency. The quiet is the story: with Europe's fiscal stress still dominating, sterling keeps winning the relative trade by default. Thread: the BoE's 6–3 hawkish hold stands, November's hike ~85% priced, and the 30-year gilt still sits above 6%. Friday's price action confirmed the floor-traders' logic — a market already this short doesn't have many new sellers left, so 1.3180 keeps holding on profit-taking. What it means: confirms — sterling remains the relative winner of Europe's fiscal stress, bid vs the euro and floored by BoE hike pricing. The one-sided risk is the Oct 28 Budget: if the gilt market dislikes it, real-money selling joins the existing shorts.

chapters.meaning: What changed: the yen actually firmed Friday — USD/JPY fell to 157.87 (−0.37%), the tape starting to price the widened strike campaign before the weekend. And the positioning picture sharpened: specs rebuilt JPY longs to 62,325 contracts in the week to Oct 6 (CFTC, released Friday), up from 55,440 — the yen-long crowd is growing again. Thread: the US–Japan rate gap still owns this pair — a US 10-year near 5.25% against a BoJ at 1.25%, with OIS pricing a December BoJ hike above 80% and the Oct 29–30 meeting live. PM Takaichi's 'appropriate action' intervention language is still on the tape. What it means: the tension tightens. The yield gap caps any yen rally — but Friday's escalation re-priced the haven leg, and now the yen has both a crowd and a catalyst. The dollar-side of this pair (see the USD chapter) decides the gap; the Gulf decides the fear.

chapters.meaning: What changed: the loonie held its 18-month lows into the weekend (USD/CAD 1.4257) as the two forces in its tape fought to a draw. The −68.3K jobs shock still anchors the downside: Oct 28 BoC hike odds sit at ~25%, and the ~161bp US–Canada 2Y gap (widest since Feb 2025) is the weight on every rally. Against that, Brent settled at $104.72 (+2.4% on the week) on the widened strike campaign — the oil tailwind leaning back in. Thread: the hawkish-BoC thesis is broken — the market prices the BoC on hold at best, and a currency that was trading the oil premium is now trading the rate gap. What it means: confirms — terms of trade giveth, the rate gap taketh away. Friday evening's strikes tilt the near-term balance back toward the oil side, but nothing changes the BoC math until Canada CPI Oct 21.

chapters.fx: What to watch: the spread itself — toward $5 means the geopolitical premium is truly unwinding; past $15 means Hormuz risk is back in force. For CAD, WTI is the number that moves the terms of trade; for JPY/EUR importers, Brent.
chapters.meaning: What changed: Friday evening re-priced the whole tape. Brent settled at $104.72 (+$0.44 on the day, +2.4% on the week) after Iran struck the Trafigura-chartered VLCC Gem No 2 off the UAE and the IRGC officially claimed the NV Sunshine hit, warning of 'punishment' across the region — the strike campaign is widening beyond the strait. Tehran is reviewing a proposal to reopen Hormuz within seven days; Trump's no-strike pledge (no attack before the Nov 3 midterms) still holds. Thread: ING's read from Friday stands — the market is 'reluctant to price out the geopolitical premium' above $100. What it means: the number that matters isn't either price, it's the ~$14 gap between them — roughly triple-to-quadruple the normal spread. The premium is the geopolitical/shipping risk, living in Brent (the seaborne benchmark exposed to Hormuz), while WTI (~$90.6–90.9, landlocked in Oklahoma) barely feels it. The Trump–Putin diesel deal (~4.8M tons, Treasury license through Apr 7, 2027, first Russian energy imports since 2022) is a sideshow for crude: ~6M barrels is ≈1.5 days of US demand (Pickering via CNN) — diesel fell 3%, crude barely moved. Side notes: Hurricane Isaias shut ~1.3 mbpd of Gulf output (62.9%), and China resumed refined-fuel exports post-Golden Week (3.7mt) — modest diesel relief.

chapters.fx: What to watch: a break back above $4,300 would signal the haven bid is broadening beyond dollar-weakness — historically a USD-negative, CHF/JPY-positive setup. Conversely, a hot CPI Wednesday that revives hike bets would likely knock gold back toward $4,000.
chapters.meaning: What changed: gold jumped ~1–1.4% to ~$4,170–4,190 on the full Friday package — a softer dollar, easing yields, and the evening's escalation arriving together. Thread: gold topped $5,318 in late January at the peak of the Iran escalation scare, then bled lower for months as the Fed's hawkish hold kept real yields elevated and the dollar ripped to 18-month highs — it sits ~22% below the peak. What it means: Friday was the first day in a while gold worked as both trades at once — the anti-dollar (down dollar, down yields) and the war hedge (evening strikes). For FX, firm gold is a soft headwind for USD and a quiet tell on risk appetite: when gold and a soft dollar move together into the weekend, the market is hedging the dollar, not fearing the world — unless the Sunday reopen shows otherwise.
